newsitem.title: USA: Fed needs bank supervisory role, Greenspan says.
newsitem.headline: Fed needs bank supervisory role, Greenspan says.

text.p: Financial system reform should not reduce the Federal Reserve's bank supervisory authority because the Fed needs it to guard against market disruption, Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan said on Saturday.

Speaking to the annual meeting of the Conference of State Bank Supervisors in San Diego, Calif., Greenspan noted critically that some question "not only the need for umbrella supervision (of financial firms) but also the need for the Fed's involvement in such supervision."

Greenspan, speaking to the group by teleconference, said the Fed's primary responsibility was to maintain stability in the overall U.S. financial system. Having a hand in bank supervision, including assessing the efficiency of risk management practices in bank holding companies' nonbanking activities, helps the Fed to do so.
"This obligation to protect against systemic disruptions cannot be met solely via open market operations and use of the discount window, as powerful as these tools may be," he said.
Greenspan said globalization of finance means future financial crises can be "unpredictable and unique" so the Fed must be ready to respond quickly.
The Fed chief said it was vital for the central bank to be familiar with all the details of the U.S. and foreign financial systems including payments and settlements methods.
"Thus, in order to carry out our systemic obligation, the Federal Reserve must be directly involved in the supervision of banks of all sizes," Greenspan said.
He said he backs financial reform, under debate in Congress, because conducting various financial businesses jointly lowers consumer prices and saves costs for firms.
Greenspan said large numbers of community-sized banks, whether they were state-chartered or national banks, was in itself important for the stability of the financial system.
"Just as a more highly diversified loan portfolio reduces risk to the individual bank, a more highly diversified banking structure reduces risk to the banking system as a whole," he said.
After the speech, Greenspan said he hoped to see state-charters and national banks on a level playing field.

"I hope we get federal regulations and statutes that will eliminate the potentially significant advantage of national charters over state-charters as we move towards interstate banking," he said, noting the issue was being addressed in regulations under discussion.
In his speech, Greenspan urged the regulators to remember that prudent risk-taking was part of banking and should be encouraged, even though it will lead to mistakes and some failures.

"Failure should occur, indeed does occur, as part of the natural process within our competitive economy," Greenspan said. "It is not a flaw in our financial system and certainly we should not attempt to eliminate it.
After the speech, Greenspan said banks were learning to cope with a sharp rise in personal bankruptcies and credit card delinquencies and that the economy was doing well despite this trend.
"We don't know why personal bankruptcies have soared as sharply as they have, especially considering the fact that the economy is doing so well and consumers in general are doing well," Greenspan.
